paragraphs: In Barnsley, children who cannot live with their own families are cared for by foster carers approved either by the council's in-house service, Fostering Barnsley, or by one of the independent fostering agencies listed on this page. The council says it has more than 130 fostering families, and its aim is to help local children stay close to home, their schools and the people who matter to them.

Fostering Barnsley approves carers for a wide range of arrangements, including short-term care, long-term care, emergency placements, respite sleepovers, short breaks for children with additional needs, parent and child placements and Staying at Home care for young people over 18. The council tries wherever possible to keep brothers and sisters together, and it also runs a Specialist Foster Carer pilot offering full-time therapeutic care to children with complex emotional needs. In its latest Foster Care Fortnight appeal it said many more carers are urgently needed so that each child can be matched with the right home.

Applicants complete Skills to Foster training during assessment, then have access to training all year round. Once approved, each carer has a supervising social worker, and there is a support line and an out-of-hours team, peer support groups, Mockingbird hubs and a foster carers' association. Fostering Barnsley says assessment usually takes four to six months.

On pay, the council publishes a skills fee structure: carers at Skills Level 1, where most begin, receive a minimum of £135 a week, Level 2 carers receive £210 per child a week, and Level 3 carers receive up to £390 a week, alongside allowances for things such as clothing, birthdays and holidays. The council quotes an average of £683 a week for its carers. A good next step is to talk to Fostering Barnsley and two or three of the agencies listed below, and compare the training, support and pay each one offers.
